He closed his phone and let his eyes go soft on the window. Some part of him carried a quiet [wistfulness]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="wistfulness · n. 渴望,愿望"} for the version of himself who had walked into this friendship without all this weight. That person had been [light-hearted]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="light-hearted · adj. 轻松愉快的,无忧无虑的; 随便的,漫不经心的"}, easy, unburdened by the [preoccupation]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="preoccupation · n. 全神贯注，入神; 当务之急；使人全神贯注的事物"} of wondering whether he was enough. He did not know how to return to that. But sitting here, at least, he had stopped moving [frantically]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="frantically · adv. 疯狂地;狂热地"} — and that, for now, felt like a beginning, however small, of something [psychedelic]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="psychedelic · adj. 引起幻觉的,致幻觉的; 产生迷幻效果的"} in the truest sense: a shift in how the whole picture looked.

### The Weight of Waking Up

She sat at the edge of the bed, trying to [collect myself]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="collect myself"} after another restless night. The [psychological]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="psychological · adj. 心理的; 精神的; 心理学的; 关于心理学的"} damage of the past year had settled into her bones quietly, the way cold does. She had believed in something — in him, in the project, in the version of herself that seemed to have it all figured out — and now the [disillusionment]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="disillusionment · n. 醒悟;理想破灭"} sat in her chest like a stone that refused to dissolve.

Her therapist had told her she was [psychologically]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="psychologically · adv. 心理上地;心理学地"} resilient, that she processed loss better than most. She wanted to believe that. But some mornings she still caught herself drifting back into [cloud-cuckoo-land]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="cloud-cuckoo-land · n. 脱离现实的幻境"}, replaying the old story where everything turned out fine, where the recognition finally came, where she was enough.

It was the [emotional arousal]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="emotional arousal"} that surprised her most — how a single memory could spike her pulse, flood her with heat, then leave her hollow. She had started to recognize it as a signal rather than a verdict. And slowly, hesitantly, something lighter was threading through the heaviness. When her niece called just to say "**Hooray for you!**" after hearing she'd submitted the application, she laughed — a real one. The [Impostor Syndrome]{.vocab tabindex="0" data-def="Impostor Syndrome"} was still there, whispering that she didn't deserve any of it. But for one quiet moment, she let the warmth land anyway.
